Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.
Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale then $(|M_n|)$ is a submartingale. More generally, for real $p\ge1$, if $E|M_n|^p<\infty$ for every $n\ge0$, then $(|M_n|^p)$ is a submartingale. We use $0^p=0$.

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a locally
square-integrable predictable process
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with localized
integral $H\cdot B$ in the progressively measurable version of
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]], with its measurable-full-event convention
for indistinguishability. The filtration satisfies the usual conditions and
local energy is finite almost surely on every finite horizon, as required by
the local-integrability definition. Let $\tau$ be a
stopping time [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]. Then the process
$s\mapsto(H\cdot B)_{s\wedge\tau}$ and the localized integral of the process
$1_{[0,\tau]}H$ are indistinguishable:
$$(H\cdot B)_{t\wedge\tau}=\int_0^t1_{[0,\tau]}(s)H_s\,dB_s\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0\text{, up to indistinguishability}.$$
In particular, for $H$ of finite energy this reduces to the stopping identity
of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], and for $\tau\equiv\infty$ it is the
definition of the localized integral.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a continuous-time filtration
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

1. A map $\tau:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ (infinite values allowed) is a **stopping
   time** for $(\mathcal F_t)$ when
   $$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0 .$$
2. For a stopping time $\tau$ its **stopped sigma-algebra** is
   $$\mathcal F_\tau:=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t \text{ for every }t\ge0\}.$$

The following facts are used below, and each is a direct set computation.

(a) $\mathcal F_\tau$ is a sigma-algebra: $\emptyset\cap\{\tau\le
    t\}=\emptyset\in\mathcal F_t$; for $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ one has
    $A^c\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau\le t\})\in\mathcal
    F_t$; and for a sequence $A_n\in\mathcal F_\tau$ the union satisfies
    $\bigl(\bigcup_nA_n\bigr)\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap\{\tau\le
    t\})\in\mathcal F_t$. All operations are literal, not modulo null sets, and
    no completeness of the filtration is assumed.
(b) If $\tau\equiv t_0<\infty$ is deterministic, then
    $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ is $A$ for $t\ge t_0$ and $\emptyset$ for $t<t_0$, so
    $\mathcal F_\tau=\bigcap_{t\ge t_0}\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t_0}$, where
    the last equality follows because the intersection includes its least
    member $\mathcal F_{t_0}$. If $\tau\equiv\infty$, then every test event
    $\{\tau\le t\}$ is empty and $\mathcal F_\tau=\mathcal F$.
(c) Suppose the filtration is right-continuous. Then $\tau$ is a stopping time
    if and only if $\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t>0$. Indeed
    $$\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\}$$
    (with the terms for $t-\tfrac1n<0$ read as the empty set, since
    $\tau\ge0$), which gives the forward implication; conversely
    $$\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\},$$
    and $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t$ by
    right-continuity together with monotonicity of the filtration.
(d) Under the same right-continuity assumption, for $A\in\mathcal F$ one has
    $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ if and only if $A\cap\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for
    every $t>0$: the forward implication follows from
    $A\cap\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_n(A\cap\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\})$ and the converse
    from $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_n(A\cap\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\})$ together with
    $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\mathcal F_t$.

Because the two versions of each test are interchangeable exactly when the
filtration is right-continuous, the convention is recorded here once: the
Brownian strong Markov theorem is stated for the usual augmentation, which is
right-continuous, and the raw-filtration statements use the non-strict test
directly. No choice principle is used by this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

No choice beyond the declared AC of the ambient interfaces enters the
construction: the coefficients $b,\sigma$ and the process are given data, and
the canonically localized integral is constructed in
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. The Axiom of Choice is declared because the
conditional-expectation and $L^2$ interfaces used downstream assume it, and
the countable-choice obligations inherited from those interfaces are declared
as dependencies of this item.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For each coordinate $i$, set $M^i_t=\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^tG^{ij}_s\,dW^j_s$, $Q_i(t)=\int_0^t\sum_j|G^{ij}_s|^2ds$, and $M_i^*(t)=\sup_{u\le t}|M^i_u|$. Stop at $\rho_R=\inf\{t:Q_i(t)\vee M_i^*(t)\ge R\}\wedge T$, for $R>0$. These processes are continuous and adapted, and $\{\rho_R\le t\}=\{Q_i(t)\vee M_i^*(t)\ge R\}$ for $t<T$, so $\rho_R$ is a stopping time [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]. The stopped process is a continuous square-integrable martingale by [F3]–[F4], its quadratic energy is bounded by $R$, and its path supremum is bounded by $R$. Apply [F2] to $|M^i|$ sampled on nested dyadic grids including $T$. By [F6], the grid maxima increase to the path supremum and monotone convergence passes the discrete bounds to $S_i(R):=\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|M^i_{t\wedge\rho_R}|^p\le q^p\mathbb E|M^i_{T\wedge\rho_R}|^p$, where $q=p/(p-1)$.

Apply [F1] to the stopped coordinate process. The stochastic term has mean zero because its integrand is bounded by the stopping level and has finite energy. Put $U_i(R)=\sup_{t\le T}|M^i_{t\wedge\rho_R}|$. The Hessian term is bounded by $\frac{p(p-1)}2U_i(R)^{p-2}Q_i(R)$, where $Q_i(R)=\int_0^{T\wedge\rho_R}\sum_j|G^{ij}_s|^2ds$. Therefore $S_i(R)\le q^p\frac{p(p-1)}2\,\mathbb E[U_i(R)^{p-2}Q_i(R)]$. For $p=2$, interpret $U_i(R)^0=1$, giving $S_i(R)\le C_2\mathbb E Q_i(R)$. For $p>2$, [F5] gives $S_i(R)\le C_pS_i(R)^{(p-2)/p}\bigl(\mathbb E Q_i(R)^{p/2}\bigr)^{2/p}$.

For $p=2$, step 2.1 gives the coordinate estimate. For $p>2$, if $S_i(R)=0$ it is immediate; otherwise divide the bound in step 2.1 by $S_i(R)^{(p-2)/p}$ and raise to the power $p/2$. In both cases $S_i(R)\le C_p\mathbb E Q_i(R)^{p/2}\le C_p\mathbb E(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2ds)^{p/2}$. Since $|M_t|\le\sqrt d\max_i|M^i_t|$, summing the coordinate estimates gives the required bound for the stopped vector integral with constant $C_{p,d}$.

As $R\to\infty$, finite pathwise energy and continuity make $\rho_R=T$ eventually almost surely. By [F7], Fatou's lemma passes the uniform bound of step 3.1 to $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|M_t|^p$. The constant depends only on $p,d$. AC is exactly the inherited assumption [A1].

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, finite dimensions $d,m\ge1$, and an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. Use a complete usual filtered probability
space and an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments
after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$, as in
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] and
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $b:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^d$
and $\sigma:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be Borel maps. Require
that they are bounded on every compact subset of $[0,T]\times U$ and locally
Lipschitz in the state uniformly in time: for every compact $K\subset U$ there
is $L_K<\infty$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $x,y\in K$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L_K|x-y|.$$
Let $\xi$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, take values in $U$ almost surely, be
independent of the future Brownian increments, and satisfy $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$.

For $n\ge1$, set
$$K_n=\{x\in U: |x|\le n,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)\ge n^{-1}\}.$$
When $U=\mathbb R^d$, interpret $\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)=+\infty$.
If $U^c\ne\varnothing$, the distance function is $1$-Lipschitz, so each
$K_n$ is closed; it is bounded, hence compact by Heine--Borel. For
$U=\mathbb R^d$, each $K_n$ is a closed ball and is compact as well. As $n$
increases, the radius bound increases and the distance threshold decreases, so
the sets are nested. Every $x\in U$ belongs to $\operatorname{int}K_n$ for all
sufficiently large $n$: choose $n>|x|$ and, when $U^c\ne\varnothing$,
$n^{-1}<\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)$. Thus their interiors exhaust $U$.
[[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

A **local strong solution up to exit** is the compatible family of stopped
adapted continuous processes $X^{(n)}$ and stopping times $\tau_n$
[[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] such that
$$\tau_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:X^{(n)}_t\notin\operatorname{int}K_n\}\wedge T, \qquad X^{(n)}_{t\wedge\tau_n}=\xi+\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}b(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,ds+ \int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}\sigma(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,dW_s,$$
with the equation holding indistinguishably and with $X^{(n)}$ constant after
$\tau_n$. Empty early $K_n$ simply give $\tau_n=0$. Compatibility means that
for $m\ge n$, $X^{(m)}$ stopped at $\tau_n$ equals $X^{(n)}$ up to
indistinguishability. The maximal lifetime is $\zeta=\lim_n\tau_n$; for
$t<\zeta$, the common value of $X^{(n)}_t$ for sufficiently large $n$ defines
the maximal local solution $X_t$.

This definition records a local integral equation; it does not assert that a
solution exists or that $\zeta=T$. Those are separate theorem obligations.
The local coefficient conditions allow superlinear growth; global Lipschitz
hypotheses will be imposed only on the coefficient truncations used in the
existence proof.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ be
nonempty and let $x, y \in X$. Then

$$|d(x,A) - d(y,A)| \le d(x,y),$$

with $d(\cdot,A)$ the distance to a nonempty set ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
Thus the real-valued function $u \mapsto d(u,A)$ changes by at most $d(u,v)$
between $u$ and $v$: it is **$1$-Lipschitz**.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process on $[0,T]$, where $T\ge0$, with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$. Extend $H$ by zero after $T$ when applying the global continuous-version theorem, and let
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ be the continuous version of
[[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]]. Then
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\,E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds .$$
The left-hand side is finite and does not depend on the chosen version, since
any two continuous versions are indistinguishable. Every continuous version of
the integral process satisfies the same bound. The path supremum in this
expectation means its measurable version $S_D=\sup_{q\in D}|M_q|$ on the
countable scaled dyadic grid $D$ (including both endpoints). Continuity
identifies it with the path supremum on a measurable event of probability one.
Indistinguishability here uses that full-event convention, as in the cited
continuous-version theorem, without assuming completeness of the filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For each $n$, choose scalar piecewise-linear cutoffs $\eta_n(r)$ and $\theta_n(r)$ with $\eta_n=1$ on $[0,n]$, $\eta_n=0$ on $[n+1,\infty)$, $\theta_n=0$ on $[0,(2n)^{-1}]$, and $\theta_n=1$ on $[n^{-1},\infty)$. Put $\chi_n(x)=\eta_n(|x|)\theta_n(\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c))$ on $U$, extend it by zero outside $U$, and use $\theta_n\equiv1$ when $U=\mathbb R^d$. The norm and distance functions are Lipschitz, so $\chi_n$ is Lipschitz, equals one on $K_n$, and has compact support inside $U$.

Define $b_n=\chi_n b$ and $\sigma_n=\chi_n\sigma$ on $U$, extended by zero outside $U$. On a compact neighborhood of their support the original coefficients are bounded and locally Lipschitz; a finite subcover gives a uniform local Lipschitz constant there. Their products with $\chi_n$ are therefore locally Lipschitz, including at the support boundary where the cutoff vanishes. A compactly supported locally Lipschitz map on $\mathbb R^d$ is globally Lipschitz: use a finite cover and a Lebesgue number for nearby pairs, and boundedness divided by that Lebesgue number for pairs farther apart. Thus $b_n,\sigma_n$ are globally Lipschitz and have linear growth.

By [F2], each truncated equation with coefficients $b_n,\sigma_n$ and initial value $\xi$ has a unique global strong solution $Z^n$. If $K_n=\varnothing$, take its exit time to be zero; otherwise stop at the first exit $\tau_n$ from $\operatorname{int}K_n$. For $m\ge n$, stop $Z^n,Z^m$ at the first time either leaves $\operatorname{int}K_n$. Before that stop both states lie in $K_n$, where both truncations equal $b,\sigma$.

Let $D=Z^n-Z^m$ up to the common stop $\tau$, and put $v(t)=\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|D_{s\wedge\tau}|^2$. The coefficients have a common Lipschitz constant $L_n$ on $K_n$. Hölder's integral inequality [F5] for the drift integral and [F4] for the stopped stochastic integral give $$v(t)\le 2tL_n^2\int_0^t v(s)\,ds+8L_n^2\int_0^t v(s)\,ds.$$ Since $D_0=0$, [F7] yields $v(t)=0$. Hence the truncated solutions agree until either exits $K_n$; continuity then makes those exit times equal, and $Z^m$ stopped at $\tau_n$ equals $Z^n$ stopped there.

The stopped family $X^{(n)}:=Z^n_{\cdot\wedge\tau_n}$ is compatible by step 4.1 and satisfies the stopped integral equation because each cutoff equals the original coefficients on $K_n$. Since $\bigcup_n\operatorname{int} K_n=U$, its lifetime $\zeta=\lim_n\tau_n$ and common values before $\zeta$ give a local strong solution in the sense of [F1]. Applying the same stopped difference estimate to any two local solutions proves equality up to the minimum of their lifetimes. AC is exactly [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on $[0,T]$ with
$U=(0,\infty)$. The input consists of $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfying
the Feller condition $2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, a step $h>0$, a current
transformed value $z_n\ge0$, and a finite Brownian increment $\Delta W_n$.
Set
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8},\qquad A=1+\frac{\kappa h}{2},\qquad c=z_n+\frac{\sigma}{2}\Delta W_n.$$
For valid parameters, $a>0$ and $A>0$. Compute
$$z_{n+1}=\frac{c+\sqrt{c^2+4Aah}}{2A},\qquad x_{n+1}=z_{n+1}^2.$$
This is the positive-root solution of
$$A z_{n+1}^2-cz_{n+1}-ah=0,$$
which is the drift-implicit Euler equation for the Lamperti variable
$Z=\sqrt X$ in the CIR model
$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$.

Return `invalid-input` for parameters outside the stated domain or a
non-finite input. Otherwise return `success` with $(z_{n+1},x_{n+1})$. In
exact real arithmetic the discriminant is strictly positive and the displayed
root is finite and positive for every $z_n\ge0$ and $\Delta W_n\in\mathbb R$;
the algorithm has no rejected root branch. A floating-point implementation
that cannot verify a finite positive root returns `solve-failure` and does
not advance the state. This is a specific implicit square-root update, not
the ordinary Euler–Maruyama update for $X$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

derivations.claim: For each $n$ let $D_n=\{1/n<X_0<n\}\in\mathcal F_0$, and let $\tau_n$ be the first exit from $[1/n,n]$. The events $D_n$ increase to a probability-one event because $X_0>0$ is finite. Use [F5] to extend $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ from that interval to a global $C^2$ function equal to zero off its positive support, then apply [F1] to the stopped process $X^{\tau_n}$. On $D_n$ its state stays in $[1/n,n]$, so the extended function and its derivatives agree with $f$, $f'(x)=1/(2\sqrt{x})$ and $f''(x)=-1/(4x^{3/2})$ by [F4]. The resulting drift is $$\frac{\kappa(\theta-X_t)}{2\sqrt{X_t}} -\frac{\sigma^2X_t}{8X_t^{3/2}} =\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8Z_t}-\frac\kappa2Z_t =\frac a{Z_t}-\frac\kappa2Z_t$$ and the diffusion is $\sigma/2$. The countable compact exhaustion proves the identity up to every compact exit and hence on the local solution's lifetime.
The Feller inequality implies $4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2\ge\sigma^2>0$, so $a>0$. Thus for the numerical step $A=1+\kappa h/2>0$ and $4Aah>0$.

Multiplying the drift-implicit equation by $z_+$ and collecting terms gives $Az_+^2-cz_+-ah=0$, with $c=z+\sigma\Delta W/2$. Its discriminant is $c^2+4Aah>c^2$, so [F3] gives a square root strictly larger than $|c|$. The quadratic formula gives the positive root $z_+=(c+\sqrt{c^2+4Aah})/(2A)$; the other root has negative numerator $c-\sqrt{c^2+4Aah}<0$ and positive denominator, hence is negative.

Every positive solution must be one of those two quadratic roots, and only the first is positive. Substitution verifies the displayed positive root in the original equation, so it is the unique admissible step, including when $z=0$. AC is exactly [A1].

Local smooth cutoffs allow the global Ito formula to act on sqrt(x) on each compact positive interval. Drift simplifies to (4*kappa*theta-sigma^2)/(8Z)-kappa*Z/2 and diffusion sigma/2, matching Alfonsi equations (2)-(3), PDF pp.1-2. Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on $[0,T]$ with
$U=\mathbb R^d$. The input is an autonomous drift $b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb
R^d$, diffusion $\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, initial state
$\xi$, and integer $N\ge1$ with $h=T/N\le1$. Define $t_n=nh$ and
$$b_h(x)=\frac{b(x)}{1+h|b(x)|}.$$
Return the grid values, step process, continuous interpolation, and status as
follows.

1. Set $Y_0=\xi$.
2. For $n=0,\ldots,N-1$, set $\Delta W_n=W_{t_{n+1}}-W_{t_n}$ and
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+h b_h(Y_n)+\sigma(Y_n)\Delta W_n.$$
3. Set $\bar Y_t=Y_n$ on $[t_n,t_{n+1})$, with $\bar Y_T=Y_N$, and set
$$Y_t=Y_n+(t-t_n)b_h(Y_n)+\sigma(Y_n)(W_t-W_{t_n}), \qquad t\in[t_n,t_{n+1}].$$
The shared endpoint formulas agree with the grid recursion.

If the dimensions, horizon, step count, or finite-valued coefficient inputs
are invalid, return `invalid-input` without a trajectory. Otherwise return
`success` and the sequence. In exact real arithmetic each update is a finite
vector expression, and $|h b_h(x)|\le1$, so the finite recursion has no
implicit solve or branch failure. The algorithm by itself asserts no moment,
stability, or convergence property.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space [[def-probability-measure]], each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ [[def-sigma-algebra]], and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC and the usual filtered Brownian conventions of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $G$ be a predictable
$d\times m$ matrix process on $[0,T]$ with
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}<\infty$$
for some real $p\ge2$, and let $M_t=\int_0^tG_s\,dW_s$ be its continuous
vector Itô integral. There is a finite constant $C_{p,d}$, independent of
$G$ and $T$, such that
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^p\le C_{p,d}\, \mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The derivative bound, integrated on the segment from $0$ to $x$, gives $|b(x)|\le B(1+|x|^{q+1})$ for a finite $B$. One-sided Lipschitzness with $y=0$ gives $\langle x,b(x)\rangle\le B(1+|x|^2)$, and global Lipschitzness of $\sigma$ gives $\|\sigma(x)\|_F\le B(1+|x|)$. Increase $B$ so these bounds hold with one constant. For $|x|\ge1$ they imply $\|\sigma(x)\|_F^2\le B_1|x|^2$, $\langle x,b(x)\rangle\le B_1|x|^2$, and $|b(x)|^2\le B_1|x|^{2q+2}$. Thus, whenever $1\le|x|\le N^{1/(2q)}$ and $h=T/N$, $h^2|b(x)|^2\le B_1T h|x|^2$. Fix once and for all $\Lambda\ge\max\{1,2B_1(1+T),1+\sup_{|x|\le1}(|b(x)|+\|\sigma(x)\|_F)\}$; continuity and compactness make this choice finite.

The recursion and Brownian adaptedness show by induction that $Y_k$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable for every $k$. For $0\le k<N$, define $$\alpha_k=1_{\{|Y_k|\ge1\}}\frac{\langle Y_k,\sigma(Y_k)\Delta W_k\rangle}{|Y_k|^2},\qquad S_0=0,\quad S_j=\sum_{k<j}\alpha_k\ (1\le j\le N).$$ Since $\alpha_k$ is $\mathcal F_{t_{k+1}}$-measurable, $(S_j)$ is adapted to the sampled filtration. For $0\le n\le N$, also define $$D_n=(\Lambda+|\xi|) \exp\!\left(\Lambda T+ \max_{0\le u\le n}\sum_{k=u}^{n-1} (\Lambda h+\Lambda|\Delta W_k|^2+\alpha_k)\right).$$ On $|Y_k|\ge1$, write $\alpha_k=v_k\cdot\Delta W_k$ with $v_k=\sigma(Y_k)^{\mathsf T}Y_k/|Y_k|^2$; global Lipschitzness of $\sigma$ gives $|v_k|\le\|\sigma(Y_k)\|_F/|Y_k|\le C$. Conditionally on $\mathcal F_{t_k}$ its variance is $h|v_k|^2\le C^2h$; on $|Y_k|<1$, $\alpha_k=0$. Brownian independence and the Gaussian density therefore give $\mathbb E[\alpha_k\mid\mathcal F_{t_k}]=0$ and, by completing the square in each coordinate, $$\mathbb E[e^{r\alpha_k}\mid\mathcal F_{t_k}]\le e^{C^2r^2h/2}\qquad(r\in\mathbb R).$$ Conditional Jensen shows that $e^{QS_j}$ and $e^{-QS_j}$ are nonnegative submartingales for each $Q>0$. Iterating the preceding bound with $r=2Q$ gives terminal second moments at most $e^{2C^2Q^2T}$ for both processes. Doob's $L^2$ inequality [F4] then gives $\sup_N\mathbb E e^{Q\max_{j\le N}|S_j|}<\infty$: the exponential of the maximum is bounded by the sum of the maxima of $e^{QS_j}$ and $e^{-QS_j}$, whose expectations are bounded by their $L^2$ maxima. For any $r>0$, choose $Q\ge\max(1,r)$; since $x^{r/Q}\le1+x$ for $x\ge0$, this also bounds $\sup_N\mathbb E e^{r\max_{j\le N}|S_j|}$. Finally, for $N\ge4r\Lambda T$, [F5] and $-\log(1-u)\le2u$ on $0\le u\le1/2$ give $$\mathbb E\exp\!\left(r\Lambda\sum_{k<N}|\Delta W_k|^2\right)=\prod_{k<N}(1-2r\Lambda h)^{-m/2}\le e^{2rm\Lambda T}.$$ Every suffix sum $\sum_{k=u}^{j-1}\alpha_k=S_j-S_u$ is bounded in absolute value by $2\max_{i\le N}|S_i|$. Since $$\max_{n\le N}D_n^p\le(\Lambda+|\xi|)^p e^{2p\Lambda T}\exp\!\left(p\Lambda\sum_{k<N}|\Delta W_k|^2+2p\max_{j\le N}|S_j|\right),$$ the three-factor Hölder bound [F7], the all-moment assumption on $\xi$, the square-exponential estimate with $r=3p$, and the exponential-martingale bound with $r=6p$ give a uniform moment for $\max_{n\le N}D_n^p$ when $N\ge N_0(p):=\max\{1,\lceil T\rceil,\lceil12p\Lambda T\rceil\}$. The finitely many smaller $N$ will be handled separately.

Set $a_n=(\mathbb E|Y_n|^p)^{1/p}$ for $p\ge2$. Decompose the recursion as $$Y_n=\xi+\sum_{k<n}h b_h(Y_k)+\sigma(0)W_{t_n} +\sum_{k<n}(\sigma(Y_k)-\sigma(0))\Delta W_k.$$ The drift sum has norm at most $N$ by [F1]. The last sum is a continuous Brownian Itô integral with a predictable step integrand. By [F6], global Lipschitzness of $\sigma$, and the $L^{p/2}$ triangle inequality from [F7], its $L^p$ norm is at most $$C_p\left(\sum_{k<n}h\, \|\sigma(Y_k)-\sigma(0)\|_{L^p}^2\right)^{1/2} \le C_p\left(h\sum_{k<n}a_k^2\right)^{1/2}.$$ The pointwise inequality $|u_1+\cdots+u_4|^p\le 4^{p-1}\sum_i|u_i|^p$ and the bounded $p$th moments of $W_t$ on $[0,T]$ therefore give $$a_n^2\le C_p(1+\|\xi\|_{L^p}^2+N^2) +C_ph\sum_{k<n}a_k^2.$$ Iterating this finite recurrence yields $\max_{n\le N}a_n^2\le C_p(1+\|\xi\|_{L^p}^2+N^2)e^{C_pT}$, hence $\max_{n\le N}\|Y_n\|_{L^p}\le C_p(1+N)$.

Write $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and use $\alpha_k,D_n$ from step 1.2. Define $$\Omega_n=\left\{\max_{k<n}D_k\le N^{1/(2q)},\ \max_{k<n}|\Delta W_k|\le1\right\}.$$ On $|Y_k|\le1$ and $|\Delta W_k|\le1$, [F1] gives $|Y_{k+1}|\le1+h|b(Y_k)|+\|\sigma(Y_k)\|_F\le\Lambda$. On $1\le|Y_k|\le N^{1/(2q)}$, expand the squared update. The drift cross term is at most $2B_1h|Y_k|^2$; the squared taming increment is at most $B_1Th|Y_k|^2$ by step 1.1; the diffusion square is at most $B_1|Y_k|^2|\Delta W_k|^2$; and the drift-noise cross term is at most the sum of those two square terms. The remaining cross term is exactly $2|Y_k|^2\alpha_k$. With the fixed $\Lambda$ chosen in step 1.1 large enough for these coefficients, $1+u\le e^u$ therefore gives $$|Y_{k+1}|\le |Y_k| \exp(\Lambda h+\Lambda|\Delta W_k|^2+\alpha_k).$$ Induction on $n$, starting either from $Y_0=\xi$ or from the last index with $|Y_k|\le1$, now gives $1_{\Omega_n}|Y_n|\le D_n$: the first step after such an index is at most $\Lambda$, and the later factors are bounded by the suffix sum in $D_n$.

Markov's inequality [F8] and step 1.2 imply, for any $r>0$, $$\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{n\le N}D_n>N^{1/(2q)}\right) \le N^{-r/(2q)}\mathbb E\max_{n\le N}D_n^r.$$ Also, by the finite union bound [F9] and the $r$th Gaussian moment, $\mathbb P(\max_{k<N}|\Delta W_k|>1) \le C_rN h^{r/2}=C_{r,T}N^{1-r/2}$. Choosing $r$ arbitrarily large in these bounds shows that for every $s>0$ there is $C_s$ with $\mathbb P(\Omega_N^c)\le C_sN^{-s}$ for all $N$.

For $p\ge1$, on $\Omega_N$ step 2.1 bounds $\mathbb E[1_{\Omega_N}|Y_n|^p]\le\mathbb E D_n^p\le C_p$; here $\Omega_N\subseteq\Omega_n$. On the complement, [F7] and step 1.3 give $$\mathbb E[1_{\Omega_N^c}|Y_n|^p] \le\mathbb P(\Omega_N^c)^{1/2} \|Y_n\|_{L^{2p}}^p \le C_sN^{-s/2}(1+N)^p.$$ Choose $s>2p$. This is uniformly bounded. For the finitely many small $N$ excluded in step 1.2, the finite recursion and linear growth of $\sigma$ give finite moments by induction; taking their finite maximum completes the uniform bound. For $1\le p<2$, apply Hölder on the probability space to the $p=2$ result. AC is exactly [A1].

Assume the data of [[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on
$[0,T]$, with $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$. Then a local strong solution up to
the exit time from $U$ exists on the given filtered space. It is unique up to
indistinguishability before its maximal lifetime $\zeta=\lim_n\tau_n$.
Equivalently, its stopped solutions on the compact exhaustion $K_n$ form a
compatible family as defined in that item. This theorem does not assert that
$\zeta=T$; a separate non-explosion argument is required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume AC and the usual filtered Brownian conventions of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $G$ be a predictable
$d\times m$ matrix process on $[0,T]$ with
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}<\infty$$
for some real $p\ge2$, and let $M_t=\int_0^tG_s\,dW_s$ be its continuous
vector Itô integral. There is a finite constant $C_{p,d}$, independent of
$G$ and $T$, such that
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^p\le C_{p,d}\, \mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then

$2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, and put
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8}.$$

$$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$$
on $U=(0,\infty)$, the Lamperti variable $Z_t=\sqrt{X_t}$ satisfies
$$dZ_t=\left(\frac a{Z_t}-\frac\kappa2 Z_t\right)dt+ \frac\sigma2dW_t$$
up to every compact exit time. Moreover, for every $h>0$, $z\ge0$, and
$\Delta W\in\mathbb R$, the drift-implicit step
$$z_+=z+h\left(\frac a{z_+}-\frac\kappa2z_+\right) +\frac\sigma2\Delta W$$
has exactly one positive root. It is the value defined by
[[alg-cir-lamperti-positive-implicit-scheme]]. The boundary input $z=0$ is
included for the numerical root statement; the CIR solution theorem below
uses $X_0>0$.

and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are

$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure

$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$

$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$

fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a continuous-time filtration
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

1. A map $\tau:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ (infinite values allowed) is a **stopping
   time** for $(\mathcal F_t)$ when
   $$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0 .$$
2. For a stopping time $\tau$ its **stopped sigma-algebra** is
   $$\mathcal F_\tau:=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t \text{ for every }t\ge0\}.$$

The following facts are used below, and each is a direct set computation.

(a) $\mathcal F_\tau$ is a sigma-algebra: $\emptyset\cap\{\tau\le
    t\}=\emptyset\in\mathcal F_t$; for $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ one has
    $A^c\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau\le t\})\in\mathcal
    F_t$; and for a sequence $A_n\in\mathcal F_\tau$ the union satisfies
    $\bigl(\bigcup_nA_n\bigr)\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap\{\tau\le
    t\})\in\mathcal F_t$. All operations are literal, not modulo null sets, and
    no completeness of the filtration is assumed.
(b) If $\tau\equiv t_0<\infty$ is deterministic, then
    $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ is $A$ for $t\ge t_0$ and $\emptyset$ for $t<t_0$, so
    $\mathcal F_\tau=\bigcap_{t\ge t_0}\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t_0}$, where
    the last equality follows because the intersection includes its least
    member $\mathcal F_{t_0}$. If $\tau\equiv\infty$, then every test event
    $\{\tau\le t\}$ is empty and $\mathcal F_\tau=\mathcal F$.
(c) Suppose the filtration is right-continuous. Then $\tau$ is a stopping time
    if and only if $\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t>0$. Indeed
    $$\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\}$$
    (with the terms for $t-\tfrac1n<0$ read as the empty set, since
    $\tau\ge0$), which gives the forward implication; conversely
    $$\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\},$$
    and $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t$ by
    right-continuity together with monotonicity of the filtration.
(d) Under the same right-continuity assumption, for $A\in\mathcal F$ one has
    $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ if and only if $A\cap\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for
    every $t>0$: the forward implication follows from
    $A\cap\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_n(A\cap\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\})$ and the converse
    from $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_n(A\cap\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\})$ together with
    $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\mathcal F_t$.

1.2 Define $$s(z)=\int_1^z u^{-\delta}\exp\!\left(\frac{2\kappa u^2}{\sigma^2}\right)du,\qquad z>0.$$ Then $s''(z)/s'(z)=-\delta/z+4\kappa z/\sigma^2$, and direct substitution gives $$\mathcal Ls(z)=s'(z)\left(\frac a z-\frac\kappa2z+\frac{\sigma^2}{8}\left(-\frac\delta z+\frac{4\kappa z}{\sigma^2}\right)\right)=0.$$ Fix $0<\varepsilon<z_0<R$, define $\tau_\varepsilon=\inf\{t<\zeta:Z_t\le\varepsilon\}$ and $\tau_R=\inf\{t<\zeta:Z_t\ge R\}$ (with $\inf\emptyset=\infty$), and set $\tau_{\varepsilon,R}=\tau_\varepsilon\wedge\tau_R\wedge T$. By [F5], this interval-exit time is a stopping time. Extend $s$ globally by [F7] and apply [F3] to the stopped process. The stopped stochastic integrand is bounded and has finite energy, so [F4] gives $\mathbb E s(Z_{T\wedge\tau_{\varepsilon,R}})=s(z_0)$. On $A_{\varepsilon,R}=\{\tau_\varepsilon\le T,\ \tau_\varepsilon<\tau_R\}$ the stopped value is $s(\varepsilon)$; on its complement it is at most $s(R)$. Therefore $$\mathbb P(A_{\varepsilon,R})\le\frac{s(R)-s(z_0)}{s(R)-s(\varepsilon)}.$$ Since $s'(z)=z^{-\delta}\exp(2\kappa z^2/\sigma^2)$ and $\delta\ge1$, $s(\varepsilon)\to-\infty$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Thus, for each fixed upper level $R$, the probability of reaching arbitrarily small positive levels before $R$ by time $T$ is zero. Taking a countable union over integer $R>z_0$ excludes lower-boundary termination on paths bounded above; lower-boundary termination can therefore remain only on paths with unbounded upper excursions by time $T$.

2.1 For $V(z)=z^2$, the global Itô formula gives $$\mathcal LV(z)=2zq(z)+c^2=\kappa\theta-\kappa z^2\le\kappa\theta.$$ For $0<\varepsilon<z_0<R$, stop at $\tau_{\varepsilon,R}$ as above. The stopped stochastic integral has mean zero by [F4], so the pathwise generator bound gives $$\mathbb E Z_{T\wedge\tau_{\varepsilon,R}}^2\le z_0^2+\kappa\theta T.$$ On the event of hitting $R$ before $\varepsilon$ by time $T$, the stopped value is $R$, hence $$R^2\mathbb P(\tau_R\le T,\ \tau_R<\tau_\varepsilon)\le z_0^2+\kappa\theta T.$$ For fixed $R$, as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ these upper-exit events increase to $\{\tau_R\le T\}$: on every path that reaches $R$ by $T$, the positive continuous path up to its first hit has a positive minimum. Thus $\mathbb P(\tau_R\le T)\le(z_0^2+\kappa\theta T)/R^2$, and letting $R\to\infty$ rules out upper escape by time $T$. A local solution cannot terminate while remaining in a compact subset of $(0,\infty)$, by [F2]. Step 1.2 excludes lower-boundary termination on bounded paths, and this estimate excludes paths with unbounded upper excursions; hence $Z$ is global and strictly positive on $[0,T]$.

Set $X=Z^2$. Applying [F3] to the global $C^2$ function $z\mapsto z^2$ gives $$dX_t=(2Z_tq(Z_t)+c^2)dt+2cZ_t\,dW_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t,$$ since $2a+c^2=\kappa\theta$ and $2c=\sigma$. Thus the CIR equation has a global positive strong solution. If $\widetilde X$ is any other positive local strong CIR solution with initial value $x_0$, [F1] makes $\sqrt{\widetilde X}$ a local solution of the same $q,c$ equation; local uniqueness in [F2] makes it equal to $Z$ up to every compact exit, so $\widetilde X=X$.

4.1 For any $p\ge1$, let $V_p(z)=z^{2p}$ on $(0,\infty)$. For each $0<\varepsilon<z_0<R$, use [F7] to extend $V_p$ to a global $C^2$ function agreeing on $[\varepsilon,R]$, and apply [F3] to the stopped process. Its generator on the stopped path is $$\mathcal LV_p(z)=\left(2pa+\frac{p(2p-1)\sigma^2}{4}\right)z^{2p-2}-p\kappa z^{2p}\le C_p(1+z^{2p}).$$ The stopped stochastic integral has mean zero by [F4]. For fixed $\varepsilon,R$, dominated convergence [F8] makes $u(t)=\mathbb E V_p(Z_{t\wedge\tau_{\varepsilon,R}})$ continuous, and Tonelli [F9] justifies the expectation of its time-integrated generator. Gronwall [F6] gives $$\sup_{0<\varepsilon<z_0<R}\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E V_p(Z_{t\wedge\tau_{\varepsilon,R}})\le C_{p,T}(1+z_0^{2p}).$$ Since $Z$ is global, continuous and strictly positive on $[0,T]$, these stopping times equal $T$ eventually along any sequence $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, $R\uparrow\infty$ on almost every path. Fatou's lemma [F10] then yields $\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E Z_t^{2p}<\infty$, and $X=Z^2$ gives the claimed CIR moment bound. AC is exactly [A1].

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, finite dimensions $d,m\ge1$, and an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. Use a complete usual filtered probability
space and an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments
after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$, as in
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] and
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $b:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^d$
and $\sigma:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be Borel maps. Require
that they are bounded on every compact subset of $[0,T]\times U$ and locally
Lipschitz in the state uniformly in time: for every compact $K\subset U$ there
is $L_K<\infty$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $x,y\in K$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L_K|x-y|.$$
Let $\xi$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, take values in $U$ almost surely, be
independent of the future Brownian increments, and satisfy $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$.

For $n\ge1$, set
$$K_n=\{x\in U: |x|\le n,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)\ge n^{-1}\}.$$
When $U=\mathbb R^d$, interpret $\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)=+\infty$.
If $U^c\ne\varnothing$, the distance function is $1$-Lipschitz, so each
$K_n$ is closed; it is bounded, hence compact by Heine--Borel. For
$U=\mathbb R^d$, each $K_n$ is a closed ball and is compact as well. As $n$
increases, the radius bound increases and the distance threshold decreases, so
the sets are nested. Every $x\in U$ belongs to $\operatorname{int}K_n$ for all
sufficiently large $n$: choose $n>|x|$ and, when $U^c\ne\varnothing$,
$n^{-1}<\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)$. Thus their interiors exhaust $U$.
[[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

A **local strong solution up to exit** is the compatible family of stopped
adapted continuous processes $X^{(n)}$ and stopping times $\tau_n$
[[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] such that
$$\tau_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:X^{(n)}_t\notin\operatorname{int}K_n\}\wedge T, \qquad X^{(n)}_{t\wedge\tau_n}=\xi+\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}b(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,ds+ \int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}\sigma(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,dW_s,$$
with the equation holding indistinguishably and with $X^{(n)}$ constant after
$\tau_n$. Empty early $K_n$ simply give $\tau_n=0$. Compatibility means that
for $m\ge n$, $X^{(m)}$ stopped at $\tau_n$ equals $X^{(n)}$ up to
indistinguishability. The maximal lifetime is $\zeta=\lim_n\tau_n$; for
$t<\zeta$, the common value of $X^{(n)}_t$ for sufficiently large $n$ defines
the maximal local solution $X_t$.

This definition records a local integral equation; it does not assert that a
solution exists or that $\zeta=T$. Those are separate theorem obligations.
The local coefficient conditions allow superlinear growth; global Lipschitz
hypotheses will be imposed only on the coefficient truncations used in the
existence proof.

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, $T>0$, and let $W$ and $\xi$ satisfy
the filtered Brownian hypotheses in
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] with $U=\mathbb R^d$.
Consider the autonomous SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=\xi,$$
where $b\in C^1(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to
\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ is globally Lipschitz, and for constants $L,C<\infty$
and an integer $q\ge1$,
$$\langle x-y,b(x)-b(y)\rangle\le L|x-y|^2, \qquad \|Db(x)\|\le C(1+|x|^q).$$
Suppose $\mathbb E|\xi|^p<\infty$ for every finite $p\ge1$. Then the
maximal local strong solution is global on $[0,T]$, is unique up to
indistinguishability, and for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^p<\infty.$$
The bound may depend on $p,T$, the coefficient constants, and the initial
moments. No global Lipschitz condition on the drift is assumed.

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, $T>0$, and let $b,\sigma,\xi,W$ satisfy
the coefficient, Brownian, and initial-moment hypotheses of
[[thm-superlinear-sde-global-existence-and-moments]]. For each integer
$N\ge\max(1,\lceil T\rceil)$, put $h=T/N$ and define $Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ by
[[alg-tamed-euler-superlinear-drift]]. Then for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\sup_{N\ge\max(1,\lceil T\rceil)}\ \max_{0\le n\le N}\mathbb E|Y_n|^p<\infty.$$
The bound may depend on $p,T$, the coefficient constants, and the initial
moments, but not on $N$ or $n$.

Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on $[0,T]$ with
$U=\mathbb R^d$. The input is an autonomous drift $b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb
R^d$, diffusion $\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, initial state
$\xi$, and integer $N\ge1$ with $h=T/N\le1$. Define $t_n=nh$ and
$$b_h(x)=\frac{b(x)}{1+h|b(x)|}.$$
Return the grid values, step process, continuous interpolation, and status as
follows.

1. Set $Y_0=\xi$.
2. For $n=0,\ldots,N-1$, set $\Delta W_n=W_{t_{n+1}}-W_{t_n}$ and
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+h b_h(Y_n)+\sigma(Y_n)\Delta W_n.$$
3. Set $\bar Y_t=Y_n$ on $[t_n,t_{n+1})$, with $\bar Y_T=Y_N$, and set
$$Y_t=Y_n+(t-t_n)b_h(Y_n)+\sigma(Y_n)(W_t-W_{t_n}), \qquad t\in[t_n,t_{n+1}].$$
The shared endpoint formulas agree with the grid recursion.

If the dimensions, horizon, step count, or finite-valued coefficient inputs
are invalid, return `invalid-input` without a trajectory. Otherwise return
`success` and the sequence. In exact real arithmetic each update is a finite
vector expression, and $|h b_h(x)|\le1$, so the finite recursion has no
implicit solve or branch failure. The algorithm by itself asserts no moment,
stability, or convergence property.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume AC. Work on a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let
$W=(W^1,\dots,W^m)$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] whose increments after time $s$ are
independent of $\mathcal F_s$, and let $H=(H^1,\dots,H^m)$ be a predictable
row-vector process [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T\|H_s\|_2^2ds<\infty$. For
$$M_t=\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^tH_s^j\,dW_s^j,$$
the continuous version satisfies
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t| \le16\sqrt m\,\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|H_s\|_2^2ds\right)^{1/2}.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume AC and the usual filtered Brownian conventions of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $G$ be a predictable
$d\times m$ matrix process on $[0,T]$ with
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}<\infty$$
for some real $p\ge2$, and let $M_t=\int_0^tG_s\,dW_s$ be its continuous
vector Itô integral. There is a finite constant $C_{p,d}$, independent of
$G$ and $T$, such that
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^p\le C_{p,d}\, \mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\underline Y_s=Y_n$ on $[t_n,t_{n+1})$ and $\delta_s=\widetilde Y_s-\underline Y_s$. Induction in the recursion shows $Y_n$ is $\mathcal F_{t_n}$-measurable, so the step coefficient processes are predictable. The interpolation is adapted and continuous and satisfies $\widetilde Y_t=\xi+\int_0^t\frac{b(\underline Y_s)} {1+h|b(\underline Y_s)|}\,ds +\int_0^t\sigma(\underline Y_s)\,dW_s.$ Its coefficient energies are finite by [F2]–[F3] and the polynomial growth of $b$. Hence $e_t=X_t-\widetilde Y_t$ is a continuous Brownian Itô process and [F5] applies.

1.2 On an interval $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$, $\delta_s=(s-t_n)b_h(Y_n)+\sigma(Y_n)(W_s-W_{t_n})$. For $r=2,4$, $|(s-t_n)b_h(Y_n)|\le h|b(Y_n)|$, and the Brownian increment is independent of $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ with $r$th moment $C_{r,m}(s-t_n)^{r/2}$ by [F9]. The moment bounds [F3], polynomial growth $|b(x)|\le C_1(1+|x|^{q+1})$, and linear growth of $\sigma$ give $\sup_n\mathbb E|b(Y_n)|^r<\infty$ and $\sup_n\mathbb E\|\sigma(Y_n)\|_F^r<\infty$. Since $h^r\le h^{r/2}$ for $h\le1$, these estimates imply $$\sup_{n<N}\sup_{s\in[t_n,t_{n+1}]}\mathbb E|\delta_s|^r\le C_rh^{r/2},\qquad r=2,4.$$ Also, with $b_h(y)=b(y)/(1+h|b(y)|)$, $|b(y)-b_h(y)|\le h|b(y)|^2$, so $\sup_n\mathbb E|b(Y_n)-b_h(Y_n)|^2\le Ch^2$ by [F3].

2.1 Put $G_s=\sigma(X_s)-\sigma(\underline Y_s)$ and $A_s=1+|X_s|^q+|\underline Y_s|^q$. The derivative bound and integration along the segment from $X_s$ to $\underline Y_s$ give $|b(X_s)-b(\underline Y_s)|\le C A_s|X_s-\underline Y_s|$. Since $X_s-\underline Y_s=e_s+\delta_s$, one-sided Lipschitzness gives $2\langle e_s,b(X_s)-b(\underline Y_s)\rangle =2\langle X_s-\underline Y_s,b(X_s)-b(\underline Y_s)\rangle -2\langle\delta_s,b(X_s)-b(\underline Y_s)\rangle \le C|e_s|^2+C(1+A_s^2)|\delta_s|^2.$ Here the second term uses $2A_s|\delta_s||e_s|\le |e_s|^2+A_s^2|\delta_s|^2$. The taming correction contributes at most $|e_s|^2+|b(\underline Y_s)-b_h(\underline Y_s)|^2$, and $\|G_s\|_F^2\le C(|e_s|^2+|\delta_s|^2)$ by global Lipschitzness of $\sigma$. Thus a nonnegative $H_s=C\bigl(|e_s|^2+(1+A_s^2)|\delta_s|^2+|b(\underline Y_s)-b_h(\underline Y_s)|^2\bigr)$ satisfies $$2\langle e_s,b(X_s)-b_h(\underline Y_s)\rangle+\|G_s\|_F^2\le H_s.$$ By [F2]–[F3], Cauchy--Schwarz [F7], and the $r=2,4$ increment estimates in step 1.2, Tonelli [F10] gives $\mathbb E\int_0^t H_sds\le C\int_0^t v(s)ds+Ch$, where $v(t)=\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|e_s|^2$.

The martingale in Itô's identity is $M_t=2\int_0^t e_s^{\mathsf T}G_s\,dW_s$. By [F6], $\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|M_s| \le32\sqrt m\, \mathbb E\left[\sup_{s\le t}|e_s| \left(\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2ds\right)^{1/2}\right].$ Using Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] and $uv\le\varepsilon u^2+(4\varepsilon)^{-1}v^2$ (which follows by expanding $(\sqrt\varepsilon u-v/(2\sqrt\varepsilon))^2\ge0$), the Lipschitz bound on $\sigma$, and step 1.2, this is at most $\tfrac12v(t)+C\int_0^t v(s)ds+Ch$.

3.1 For each finite $N$, [F2] and [F11] give $\mathbb E\sup_{s\le T}|e_s|^2<\infty$, and [F12] makes $v(t)$ continuous. Taking the supremum over times up to $t$ in Itô's identity [F5], the pointwise majorant in step 2.1 gives $\sup_{u\le t}\int_0^u H_sds\le\int_0^tH_sds$; now take expectations and insert steps 2.1–2.2. Moving $v(t)/2$ to the left gives $v(t)\le C\int_0^t v(s)ds+Ch$. Gronwall [F8] yields $v(T)\le C_T h$. AC is inherited exactly through [A1], so the stated strong order follows.
