Let $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfy the Feller condition
$2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, and put
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8}.$$
For a positive local strong solution of the CIR SDE
$$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$$
on $U=(0,\infty)$, the Lamperti variable $Z_t=\sqrt{X_t}$ satisfies
$$dZ_t=\left(\frac a{Z_t}-\frac\kappa2 Z_t\right)dt+ \frac\sigma2dW_t$$
up to every compact exit time. Moreover, for every $h>0$, $z\ge0$, and
$\Delta W\in\mathbb R$, the drift-implicit step
$$z_+=z+h\left(\frac a{z_+}-\frac\kappa2z_+\right) +\frac\sigma2\Delta W$$
has exactly one positive root. It is the value defined by
[[alg-cir-lamperti-positive-implicit-scheme]]. The boundary input $z=0$ is
included for the numerical root statement; the CIR solution theorem below
uses $X_0>0$.

Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on $[0,T]$ with
$U=(0,\infty)$. The input consists of $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfying
the Feller condition $2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, a step $h>0$, a current
transformed value $z_n\ge0$, and a finite Brownian increment $\Delta W_n$.
Set
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8},\qquad A=1+\frac{\kappa h}{2},\qquad c=z_n+\frac{\sigma}{2}\Delta W_n.$$
For valid parameters, $a>0$ and $A>0$. Compute
$$z_{n+1}=\frac{c+\sqrt{c^2+4Aah}}{2A},\qquad x_{n+1}=z_{n+1}^2.$$
This is the positive-root solution of
$$A z_{n+1}^2-cz_{n+1}-ah=0,$$
which is the drift-implicit Euler equation for the Lamperti variable
$Z=\sqrt X$ in the CIR model
$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$.

Return `invalid-input` for parameters outside the stated domain or a
non-finite input. Otherwise return `success` with $(z_{n+1},x_{n+1})$. In
exact real arithmetic the discriminant is strictly positive and the displayed
root is finite and positive for every $z_n\ge0$ and $\Delta W_n\in\mathbb R$;
the algorithm has no rejected root branch. A floating-point implementation
that cannot verify a finite positive root returns `solve-failure` and does
not advance the state. This is a specific implicit square-root update, not
the ordinary Euler–Maruyama update for $X$.

Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]]. Let
$\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$, let $x_0>0$ be deterministic, and suppose
$2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$. Then the CIR SDE
$$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t, \qquad X_0=x_0,$$
has a unique global strong solution on every finite horizon. Its paths remain
strictly positive and finite, and for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E X_t^p<\infty.$$
No negative-moment bound or strong numerical convergence rate is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The exact path $Z=\sqrt X$ is continuous and strictly positive on the compact interval $[0,T]$ by [F2]. Hence its pathwise minimum is positive and its maximum is finite. For every $\eta>0$ choose $0<\varepsilon<R$ so that the event $$E_{\varepsilon,R}=\{\varepsilon\le Z_t\le R\text{ for every }t\le T\}$$ has probability at least $1-\eta$; these events increase to a probability-one event as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and $R\uparrow\infty$.

Write $c=\sigma/2$ and $$r_{n+1}=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}} \bigl(q(Z_s)-q(Z_{t_{n+1}})\bigr)ds.$$ The exact SDE and the implicit recursion give $$Z_{t_{n+1}}=Z_{t_n}+hq(Z_{t_{n+1}})+c\Delta W_n+r_{n+1}, \qquad Z_{n+1}=Z_n+hq(Z_{n+1})+c\Delta W_n.$$ Let $e_n=Z_n-Z_{t_n}$. Since $q'(z)=-a/z^2-\kappa/2\le-\kappa/2$, the mean-value theorem gives $(u-v)(q(u)-q(v))\le-\kappa|u-v|^2/2$ for positive $u,v$. Subtract the two updates and take the inner product with $e_{n+1}$: $$(1+h\kappa/2)|e_{n+1}|^2 \le |e_{n+1}|\,|e_n-r_{n+1}|.$$ If $e_{n+1}=0$ the next bound is immediate; otherwise divide by $(1+h\kappa/2)|e_{n+1}|$ to get $|e_{n+1}|\le|e_n|+|r_{n+1}|$. As $e_0=0$, $\max_{n\le N}|e_n|\le\sum_{n<N}|r_{n+1}|$.

On $E_{\varepsilon,R}$, the drift $q$ is bounded by $B$ and is Lipschitz with a constant $L$. For $s\in[t_n,t_{n+1}]$, the exact transformed equation gives $$|Z_s-Z_{t_{n+1}}| \le Bh+c|W_s-W_{t_{n+1}}|.$$ A centered normal variable of variance $v>0$ has absolute first moment $\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi v}}\int_0^\infty x e^{-x^2/(2v)}dx=\sqrt{2v/\pi}$ by direct integration of its density; at $v=0$ both sides are zero. Thus, using $1_{E_{\varepsilon,R}}\le1$ (without assuming independence of this path event from the increment) and [F3], $$\mathbb E[1_{E_{\varepsilon,R}}|r_{n+1}|] \le L\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}} \left(Bh+c\sqrt{2(t_{n+1}-s)/\pi}\right)ds \le C_{\varepsilon,R}(h^2+h^{3/2}).$$ Summing over $n<N$ and using $Nh=T$ gives $\mathbb E[1_{E_{\varepsilon,R}}\sum_{n<N}|r_{n+1}|] \le C_{\varepsilon,R,T}\sqrt h$.

For any $\rho>0$, steps 1.2–2.1 and [F4] give $$\mathbb P\left(\max_{n\le N}|e_n|>\rho\right) \le\mathbb P(E_{\varepsilon,R}^c) +\rho^{-1}C_{\varepsilon,R,T}\sqrt h.$$ First let $N\to\infty$ with $\varepsilon,R$ fixed, then let $\eta\to0$ using step 1.1. Thus $\max_n|Z_n-Z_{t_n}|\to0$ in probability. On $E_{\varepsilon,R}\cap\{\max_n|e_n|\le1\}$, $|Z_n+Z_{t_n}|\le2R+1$, and hence $$\max_n|X_n^h-X_{t_n}| \le(2R+1)\max_n|Z_n-Z_{t_n}|.$$ The probability of the complementary event is arbitrarily small by the event construction in step 1.1 and the convergence just proved. This gives the stated convergence in probability for $X_n^h=Z_n^2$. No $L^p$ rate follows from this localization argument. AC is exactly [A1].

Let $d\ge1$, let $f:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous, and suppose for every fixed $t$ and all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\langle f(t,x)-f(t,y),x-y\rangle\le-\mu\|x-y\|_2^2$$

for some $\mu\ge0$. For every $h>0$, define $H_{t,h}(x)=x-hf(t,x)$. Then $H_{t,h}$ is bijective and its inverse $R_{t,h}=H_{t,h}^{-1}$, the backward Euler step map, satisfies

$$\|R_{t,h}(u)-R_{t,h}(v)\|_2\le\frac{1}{1+h\mu}\|u-v\|_2.$$

In particular, for each input state $u$, the equation $z=u+h f(t,z)$ has exactly one solution on all of $\mathbb R^d$. No $hL<1$ contraction assumption is needed for this dissipative branch.

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, $T>0$, and let $W$ and $\xi$ satisfy
the filtered Brownian hypotheses in
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] with $U=\mathbb R^d$.
Consider the autonomous SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=\xi,$$
where $b\in C^1(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to
\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ is globally Lipschitz, and for constants $L,C<\infty$
and an integer $q\ge1$,
$$\langle x-y,b(x)-b(y)\rangle\le L|x-y|^2, \qquad \|Db(x)\|\le C(1+|x|^q).$$
Suppose $\mathbb E|\xi|^p<\infty$ for every finite $p\ge1$. Then the
maximal local strong solution is global on $[0,T]$, is unique up to
indistinguishability, and for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^p<\infty.$$
The bound may depend on $p,T$, the coefficient constants, and the initial
moments. No global Lipschitz condition on the drift is assumed.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, finite dimensions $d,m\ge1$, and an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. Use a complete usual filtered probability
space and an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments
after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$, as in
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] and
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $b:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^d$
and $\sigma:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be Borel maps. Require
that they are bounded on every compact subset of $[0,T]\times U$ and locally
Lipschitz in the state uniformly in time: for every compact $K\subset U$ there
is $L_K<\infty$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $x,y\in K$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L_K|x-y|.$$
Let $\xi$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, take values in $U$ almost surely, be
independent of the future Brownian increments, and satisfy $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$.

For $n\ge1$, set
$$K_n=\{x\in U: |x|\le n,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)\ge n^{-1}\}.$$
When $U=\mathbb R^d$, interpret $\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)=+\infty$.
If $U^c\ne\varnothing$, the distance function is $1$-Lipschitz, so each
$K_n$ is closed; it is bounded, hence compact by Heine--Borel. For
$U=\mathbb R^d$, each $K_n$ is a closed ball and is compact as well. As $n$
increases, the radius bound increases and the distance threshold decreases, so
the sets are nested. Every $x\in U$ belongs to $\operatorname{int}K_n$ for all
sufficiently large $n$: choose $n>|x|$ and, when $U^c\ne\varnothing$,
$n^{-1}<\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)$. Thus their interiors exhaust $U$.
[[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

A **local strong solution up to exit** is the compatible family of stopped
adapted continuous processes $X^{(n)}$ and stopping times $\tau_n$
[[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] such that
$$\tau_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:X^{(n)}_t\notin\operatorname{int}K_n\}\wedge T, \qquad X^{(n)}_{t\wedge\tau_n}=\xi+\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}b(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,ds+ \int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}\sigma(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,dW_s,$$
with the equation holding indistinguishably and with $X^{(n)}$ constant after
$\tau_n$. Empty early $K_n$ simply give $\tau_n=0$. Compatibility means that
for $m\ge n$, $X^{(m)}$ stopped at $\tau_n$ equals $X^{(n)}$ up to
indistinguishability. The maximal lifetime is $\zeta=\lim_n\tau_n$; for
$t<\zeta$, the common value of $X^{(n)}_t$ for sufficiently large $n$ defines
the maximal local solution $X_t$.

This definition records a local integral equation; it does not assert that a
solution exists or that $\zeta=T$. Those are separate theorem obligations.
The local coefficient conditions allow superlinear growth; global Lipschitz
hypotheses will be imposed only on the coefficient truncations used in the
existence proof.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume AC and the usual filtered Brownian conventions of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $G$ be a predictable
$d\times m$ matrix process on $[0,T]$ with
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}<\infty$$
for some real $p\ge2$, and let $M_t=\int_0^tG_s\,dW_s$ be its continuous
vector Itô integral. There is a finite constant $C_{p,d}$, independent of
$G$ and $T$, such that
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^p\le C_{p,d}\, \mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds\right)^{p/2}.$$

Assume AC. Work on a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let
$W=(W^1,\dots,W^m)$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] whose increments after time $s$ are
independent of $\mathcal F_s$, and let $H=(H^1,\dots,H^m)$ be a predictable
row-vector process [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T\|H_s\|_2^2ds<\infty$. For
$$M_t=\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^tH_s^j\,dW_s^j,$$
the continuous version satisfies
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t| \le16\sqrt m\,\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|H_s\|_2^2ds\right)^{1/2}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$ for every finite $T$. Then there is an
adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous paths such that
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ almost surely for every $t\ge0$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]], and $M$ is a
square-integrable martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]: $EM_t^2=E\int_0^tH_s^2ds<\infty$
for every $t$. Any two such continuous versions agree at every time on one
measurable event of probability one; in particular the continuous version is
unique in this common-full-measure-event sense, and it is the only continuous
square-integrable martingale whose value at each deterministic $t$ is the
integral class.

This conclusion is deliberately distinguished from the exact definition of
indistinguishability in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. On a
noncomplete probability space the full equality set, although it contains the
measurable probability-one event constructed below, need not itself be
measurable. On a complete probability space the two notions coincide, because
the complement of the equality set is then a measurable subset of a null set.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: First prove stability. For two updates with difference $e_n=Y_n-\widetilde Y_n$, the resolvent estimate [F1] and Brownian independence give $$\begin{aligned} \mathbb E(|e_{n+1}|^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}) &\le(1+h\mu)^{-2} \mathbb E\left(|e_n+ (\sigma(Y_n)-\sigma(\widetilde Y_n))\Delta W_n|^2 \mid\mathcal F_{t_n}\right)\\ &\le(1+hL_\sigma^2)|e_n|^2. \end{aligned}$$ The cross term vanishes because $e_n$ and the diffusion difference are $\mathcal F_{t_n}$-measurable and $\Delta W_n$ is independent with mean zero; its covariance is $hI_m$. Iterating and using $(1+hL_\sigma^2)^n\le e^{L_\sigma^2t_n}$ proves the second estimate.

1.2 Let $X_n=X_{t_n}$ and define $$d_{n+1}=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(b(X_s)-b(X_{n+1}))ds, \qquad m_{n+1}=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(\sigma(X_s)-\sigma(X_n))dW_s.$$ The SDE integral equation gives $X_{n+1}-hb(X_{n+1})=X_n+\sigma(X_n)\Delta W_n+d_{n+1}+m_{n+1}$. With $R_h=(I-hb)^{-1}$, the numerical update and [F1] therefore imply, for $e_n=Y_n-X_n$, $$|e_{n+1}|\le|e_n+\xi_{n+1}-d_{n+1}|, \qquad \xi_{n+1}=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(\sigma(Y_n)-\sigma(X_s))dW_s.$$ The identity for $\xi_{n+1}$ follows by adding and subtracting $\sigma(X_n)\Delta W_n$. Its conditional mean given $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ is zero by [F9].

1.3 From [F2], linear growth of $\sigma$, and the SDE equation, for $r=2,4$ and $s\in[t_n,t_{n+1}]$, $$\mathbb E|X_s-X_n|^r\le C_r h^{r/2}.$$ Indeed the drift increment has $r$th moment at most $h^{r-1}\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\mathbb E|b(X_u)|^rdu\le C h^r$ by Hölder and [F10], while [F4] bounds the stochastic increment by $C_r\mathbb E(\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\|\sigma(X_u)\|_F^2du)^{r/2} \le C_rh^{r/2}$. The polynomial local-Lipschitz estimate [F5], all moments in [F2], and Hölder [F6] then give $$\mathbb E|d_{n+1}|^2\le C h^3.$$ The isometry [F3] and global Lipschitzness of $\sigma$ give the unconditional bound $$\mathbb E|\xi_{n+1}|^2\le C h\mathbb E|e_n|^2+C h^2.$$

2.1 Squaring the error inequality in step 1.2 and applying $2|e_n||d_{n+1}|\le h|e_n|^2+h^{-1}|d_{n+1}|^2$ and $2|\xi_{n+1}||d_{n+1}|\le|\xi_{n+1}|^2+|d_{n+1}|^2$ gives $$|e_{n+1}|^2\le(1+h)|e_n|^2+ 2\langle e_n,\xi_{n+1}\rangle+ 2|\xi_{n+1}|^2+(2+h^{-1})|d_{n+1}|^2.$$ By [F9], the increments $\xi_{n+1}$ are martingale differences. Summing their unconditional second-moment bound from step 1.3 gives $\sum_{n<N}\mathbb E|\xi_{n+1}|^2 \le Ch\sum_{n<N}\mathbb E|e_n|^2+Ch$; step 1.3 also gives $\sum_{n<N}(2+h^{-1})\mathbb E|d_{n+1}|^2\le Ch$.

2.2 Put $v_j=\mathbb E\max_{k\le j}|e_k|^2$ for $0\le j\le N$. For each $j\le N$, the partial sums $M_j=2\sum_{n<j}\langle e_n,\xi_{n+1}\rangle$ form a martingale by [F9]. Written as one Brownian Itô integral, its integrand on $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$ is $2e_n^{\mathsf T}(\sigma(Y_n)-\sigma(X_s))$. The $L^1$ maximal bound [F4] gives $$\mathbb E\max_{l\le j}|M_l|\le32\sqrt m\,\mathbb E\left[\max_{n<j}|e_n|\left(\sum_{n<j}\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\|\sigma(Y_n)-\sigma(X_s)\|_F^2ds\right)^{1/2}\right].$$ Applying $uv\le\varepsilon u^2+(4\varepsilon)^{-1}v^2$ (obtained by expanding $(\sqrt\varepsilon u-v/(2\sqrt\varepsilon))^2\ge0$) factors out the error maximum and yields, for any $\varepsilon>0,$ $$\mathbb E\max_{l\le j}|M_l|\le\varepsilon v_{j-1}+C_\varepsilon\mathbb E\sum_{n<j}\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\|\sigma(Y_n)-\sigma(X_s)\|_F^2ds.$$ By Lipschitzness, $\|\sigma(Y_n)-\sigma(X_s)\|_F^2\le2L_\sigma^2(|e_n|^2+|X_s-X_n|^2)$. Step 1.3 and Tonelli [F10] then give $$\mathbb E\max_{l\le j}|M_l|\le\varepsilon v_{j-1}+C_\varepsilon h\sum_{n<j}\mathbb E|e_n|^2+C_\varepsilon h,$$ since $\sum_{n<j}\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\mathbb E|X_s-X_n|^2ds\le Ch$.

Recall $v_j$ from step 2.2; $e_0=0$ because both methods start from $\xi$. Subtract $|e_n|^2$ from both sides of step 2.1 and sum from $n=0$ to $j-1$. Taking the maximum over partial endpoints makes the martingale term $\max_{l\le j}|M_l|$; the remaining nonnegative terms have expectation at most $C h\sum_{k<j}v_k+Ch$ by the local bounds in steps 1.3--2.2. Use step 2.2 with $\varepsilon=1/2$; since $v_{j-1}\le v_j$, absorb the martingale contribution to obtain $$v_j\le C h\sum_{k<j}v_k+Ch.$$ Choose $C_0\ge C$ so this implies $v_j\le C_0w_j$ for $w_j=h+h\sum_{k<j}v_k$. Then $w_{j+1}=w_j+hv_j\le(1+C_0h)w_j$ and $w_0=h$, so $v_N\le C_0h(1+C_0h)^N\le C_0e^{C_0T}h$. This proves the first assertion; the stability assertion was proved in step 1.1. AC is exactly [A1].

Assume AC. Fix finite integers $d,m\ge1$, $T>0$, and $N\ge1$ such that
$h=T/N\le1$. Work on a filtered probability space whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be an adapted standard
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments after time $s$ are
independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Let $X_0$ be finite, $\mathcal F_0$-measurable,
and independent of $\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.
Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be $C^1$. Assume finite constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2,\qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2,$$
$$|f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2.$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius
norm.

Set $t_k=kh$ and construct the grid approximation recursively by
$$Y_0=X_0,\qquad Y_{k+1}=Y_k+f(Y_k)h+g(Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}),\quad 0\le k<N.$$
The output also includes the left-endpoint step process
$$\bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N,$$
and the continuous interpolation
$$Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}).$$
The recursion makes the two interpolation formulas agree at every shared
endpoint. The finite recursion is defined pathwise: $C^1$ coefficients are
finite-valued, each $Y_k$ is finite almost surely by induction, and Brownian
paths are continuous. This algorithm defines no moment or convergence claim.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, $T>0$, and let $W$ and $\xi$ satisfy
the filtered Brownian hypotheses in
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] with $U=\mathbb R^d$.
Consider the autonomous SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=\xi,$$
where $b\in C^1(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to
\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ is globally Lipschitz, and for constants $L,C<\infty$
and an integer $q\ge1$,
$$\langle x-y,b(x)-b(y)\rangle\le L|x-y|^2, \qquad \|Db(x)\|\le C(1+|x|^q).$$
Suppose $\mathbb E|\xi|^p<\infty$ for every finite $p\ge1$. Then the
maximal local strong solution is global on $[0,T]$, is unique up to
indistinguishability, and for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^p<\infty.$$
The bound may depend on $p,T$, the coefficient constants, and the initial
moments. No global Lipschitz condition on the drift is assumed.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, finite dimensions $d,m\ge1$, and an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. Use a complete usual filtered probability
space and an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments
after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$, as in
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] and
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $b:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^d$
and $\sigma:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be Borel maps. Require
that they are bounded on every compact subset of $[0,T]\times U$ and locally
Lipschitz in the state uniformly in time: for every compact $K\subset U$ there
is $L_K<\infty$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $x,y\in K$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L_K|x-y|.$$
Let $\xi$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, take values in $U$ almost surely, be
independent of the future Brownian increments, and satisfy $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$.

For $n\ge1$, set
$$K_n=\{x\in U: |x|\le n,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)\ge n^{-1}\}.$$
When $U=\mathbb R^d$, interpret $\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)=+\infty$.
If $U^c\ne\varnothing$, the distance function is $1$-Lipschitz, so each
$K_n$ is closed; it is bounded, hence compact by Heine--Borel. For
$U=\mathbb R^d$, each $K_n$ is a closed ball and is compact as well. As $n$
increases, the radius bound increases and the distance threshold decreases, so
the sets are nested. Every $x\in U$ belongs to $\operatorname{int}K_n$ for all
sufficiently large $n$: choose $n>|x|$ and, when $U^c\ne\varnothing$,
$n^{-1}<\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)$. Thus their interiors exhaust $U$.
[[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

A **local strong solution up to exit** is the compatible family of stopped
adapted continuous processes $X^{(n)}$ and stopping times $\tau_n$
[[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] such that
$$\tau_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:X^{(n)}_t\notin\operatorname{int}K_n\}\wedge T, \qquad X^{(n)}_{t\wedge\tau_n}=\xi+\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}b(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,ds+ \int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}\sigma(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,dW_s,$$
with the equation holding indistinguishably and with $X^{(n)}$ constant after
$\tau_n$. Empty early $K_n$ simply give $\tau_n=0$. Compatibility means that
for $m\ge n$, $X^{(m)}$ stopped at $\tau_n$ equals $X^{(n)}$ up to
indistinguishability. The maximal lifetime is $\zeta=\lim_n\tau_n$; for
$t<\zeta$, the common value of $X^{(n)}_t$ for sufficiently large $n$ defines
the maximal local solution $X_t$.

This definition records a local integral equation; it does not assert that a
solution exists or that $\zeta=T$. Those are separate theorem obligations.
The local coefficient conditions allow superlinear growth; global Lipschitz
hypotheses will be imposed only on the coefficient truncations used in the
existence proof.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The drift $b(x)=-x^3$ satisfies $(x-y)(b(x)-b(y))=-(x-y)^2(x^2+xy+y^2)\le0$, since $x^2+xy+y^2=(x+y/2)^2+3y^2/4\ge0$. Also $|b'(x)|=3x^2\le3(1+|x|^2)$, and $\sigma(x)=1$ is globally Lipschitz. Thus [F3] applies with deterministic $X_0=0$, so $\mathbb E|X_T|^p<\infty$ for every finite $p\ge1$.

The algorithm [F1] gives the displayed recursion. For $h\le1/4$, set $$E_N=\{h^{-1}\le\Delta W_0\le2h^{-1}\}\cap \bigcap_{n=1}^{N-1}\{|\Delta W_n|\le1\}.$$ The increments are independent by [F2]. The normal density, bounded below on $[h^{-1},2h^{-1}]$ by its value at $2h^{-1}$, gives $$\mathbb P(h^{-1}\le\Delta W_0\le2h^{-1}) \ge(2\pi)^{-1/2}h^{-3/2}e^{-2h^{-3}}.$$ Also $\mathbb P(|\Delta W_n|>1)\le\mathbb E|\Delta W_n|^2=h$, since $1_{\{|z|>1\}}\le |z|^2$. For $h\le1/4$, $(1-h)^{N-1}\ge e^{-2h(N-1)}\ge e^{-2T}$. Hence $$\mathbb P(E_N)\ge (2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-2T}h^{-3/2}e^{-2h^{-3}}.$$

On $E_N$, $Y_1=\Delta W_0\ge h^{-1}$. If $|y|\ge h^{-1}$ and $|\delta|\le1$, then $$|y-hy^3+\delta|\ge h|y|^3-|y|-1 =h|y|^3\left(1-\frac1{h|y|^2}-\frac1{h|y|^3}\right) \ge\frac h2|y|^3,$$ because the two fractions are at most $h$ and $h^2$, whose sum is at most $5/16<1/2$. The lower bound is at least $h^{-1}$ when $h\le1/2$ and $|y|\ge h^{-1}$. Induction therefore gives $|Y_n|\ge h^{-1}$ for all $1\le n\le N$ on $E_N$. With $z_n=\sqrt{h/2}|Y_n|$, the same inequality gives $z_{n+1}\ge z_n^3$, while $z_1\ge(2h)^{-1/2}>1$. Thus $$|Y_N|\ge\sqrt{2/h}\,(2h)^{-3^{N-1}/2}\quad\text{on }E_N.$$

Combining steps 1.2 and 2.1 yields $$\mathbb E|Y_N|^p\ge(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-2T}h^{-3/2}e^{-2h^{-3}} \left(\sqrt{2/h}\,(2h)^{-3^{N-1}/2}\right)^p.$$ Here $h=T/N$. The positive logarithmic term $\frac p2 3^{N-1}\log((2h)^{-1})$ grows faster than the negative term $2h^{-3}=2N^3/T^3$, so this lower bound tends to $+\infty$. AC is exactly [A1].

Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on $[0,T]$ with
$U=(0,\infty)$. The input consists of $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfying
the Feller condition $2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, a step $h>0$, a current
transformed value $z_n\ge0$, and a finite Brownian increment $\Delta W_n$.
Set
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8},\qquad A=1+\frac{\kappa h}{2},\qquad c=z_n+\frac{\sigma}{2}\Delta W_n.$$
For valid parameters, $a>0$ and $A>0$. Compute
$$z_{n+1}=\frac{c+\sqrt{c^2+4Aah}}{2A},\qquad x_{n+1}=z_{n+1}^2.$$
This is the positive-root solution of
$$A z_{n+1}^2-cz_{n+1}-ah=0,$$
which is the drift-implicit Euler equation for the Lamperti variable
$Z=\sqrt X$ in the CIR model
$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$.

Return `invalid-input` for parameters outside the stated domain or a
non-finite input. Otherwise return `success` with $(z_{n+1},x_{n+1})$. In
exact real arithmetic the discriminant is strictly positive and the displayed
root is finite and positive for every $z_n\ge0$ and $\Delta W_n\in\mathbb R$;
the algorithm has no rejected root branch. A floating-point implementation
that cannot verify a finite positive root returns `solve-failure` and does

Let $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfy the Feller condition
$2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, and put
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8}.$$
For a positive local strong solution of the CIR SDE
$$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$$
on $U=(0,\infty)$, the Lamperti variable $Z_t=\sqrt{X_t}$ satisfies
$$dZ_t=\left(\frac a{Z_t}-\frac\kappa2 Z_t\right)dt+ \frac\sigma2dW_t$$
up to every compact exit time. Moreover, for every $h>0$, $z\ge0$, and
$\Delta W\in\mathbb R$, the drift-implicit step
$$z_+=z+h\left(\frac a{z_+}-\frac\kappa2z_+\right) +\frac\sigma2\Delta W$$
has exactly one positive root. It is the value defined by
[[alg-cir-lamperti-positive-implicit-scheme]]. The boundary input $z=0$ is
included for the numerical root statement; the CIR solution theorem below
uses $X_0>0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Brownian motion here means the finite-horizon version of the cited definition:
$W_0=0$ almost surely, with continuous paths and the stated increments on
$[0,T]$. All cited stochastic-calculus interfaces are used on this interval.
Their constructions require no extension of $W$ beyond $T$: elementary
integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their
$L^2$ limits and continuous versions are constructed on that same interval.
For a predictable scalar integrand $H$ with finite pathwise energy, localize
at $\rho_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:\int_0^t H_s^2ds\ge n\}\wedge T$.
Here $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$.
The stopped integrands have expected energy at most $n$; their continuous
integrals agree up to the smaller stop by the finite-energy stopping identity.
On the full event of finite energy, $\rho_n=T$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, so these integrals paste uniquely on the whole closed interval $[0,T]$,
exactly as in the localized construction of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. Fix finite integers $d,m\ge1$, $T>0$, and $N\ge1$ such that
$h=T/N\le1$. Work on a filtered probability space whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be an adapted standard
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments after time $s$ are
independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Let $X_0$ be finite, $\mathcal F_0$-measurable,
and independent of $\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.
Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be $C^1$. Assume finite constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2,\qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2,$$
$$|f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2.$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius
norm.

Set $t_k=kh$ and construct the grid approximation recursively by
$$Y_0=X_0,\qquad Y_{k+1}=Y_k+f(Y_k)h+g(Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}),\quad 0\le k<N.$$
The output also includes the left-endpoint step process
$$\bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N,$$
and the continuous interpolation
$$Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}).$$
The recursion makes the two interpolation formulas agree at every shared
endpoint. The finite recursion is defined pathwise: $C^1$ coefficients are
finite-valued, each $Y_k$ is finite almost surely by induction, and Brownian
paths are continuous. This algorithm defines no moment or convergence claim.

Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on $[0,T]$ with
$U=\mathbb R^d$. An admissible mathematical input has finite dimensions
$d,m\ge1$, $T>0$, $N\ge1$ with $h=T/N\le1$, an autonomous continuous drift
$b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, a finite-valued Borel diffusion
$\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, and a finite
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable initial state $\xi$. It also has a constant
$\mu\ge0$ such that
$$\langle x-y,b(x)-b(y)\rangle\le-\mu|x-y|^2\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$
This global condition is a precondition on the mathematical input, not a
runtime test over all $x,y$. For $h>0$, set $H_h(x)=x-hb(x)$ and let
$R_h=H_h^{-1}$, which is defined uniquely on all of $\mathbb R^d$ by
[[thm-backward-euler-dissipative-resolvent-contraction]].

First check that $d,m$ are positive integers, $T$ is finite and positive,
$N$ is a positive integer, $0<h=T/N\le1$, and $\xi$ is finite. If any of
these checks fails, return `invalid-input`. An exact execution then sets
$Y_0=\xi$ and, for $n=0,\ldots,N-1$, computes
$$u_n=Y_n+\sigma(Y_n)(W_{t_{n+1}}-W_{t_n}),\qquad Y_{n+1}=R_h(u_n).$$
It returns the grid values, the left-endpoint step process
$$\bar Y_t=Y_n\quad(t_n\le t<t_{n+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N,$$
and the continuous interpolation
$$Y_t=Y_n+(t-t_n)b(Y_{n+1})+\sigma(Y_n)(W_t-W_{t_n}), \qquad t_n\le t\le t_{n+1}.$$
This is a pathwise continuous extension of the grid values. At each shared
endpoint the interpolation agrees with the grid update.

A finite implementation may instead receive a root-solver interface $S$ and
an integer work cap $M\ge0$. Each call $S(H_h,u_n,M)$ must terminate after at
most $M$ declared solver iterations and return either
`certified-root(z, proof)` or `no-certificate(last-iterate, residual)` (with
`last-iterate = null` if the cap permits no iterate). The
supplied exact verifier must terminate and accepts a certificate precisely when it proves that
$z\in\mathbb R^d$ is finite and $H_h(z)=u_n$. At the first call returning
`no-certificate`, or at the first certificate rejected by the verifier, stop
and return `solve-failure` with zero-based failed index $n$, the valid grid prefix through
$Y_n$, the step process on $[0,t_n]$, the interpolation on $[0,t_n]$, and the
solver diagnostic. For `no-certificate`, retain its last iterate and residual;
for a rejected certificate with candidate $z$, report $z$ and residual
$H_h(z)-u_n$. If the diagnostic has no finite candidate, its iterate and
residual are null. Do not assign $Y_{n+1}$ or continue. A
verified root equals $R_h(u_n)$ by uniqueness. If every call is verified,
return `success` and the exact grid, step process, and interpolation above.
The global dissipativity condition remains an admissibility precondition and
is not tested by these finite-value checks. Thus a failed finite solve records
failure of certification, not absence of a mathematical root.
The algorithm makes no convergence or mean-square stability claim.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Define $X_t=\exp(-7t/2+\sqrt3W_t)$. Itô's formula [F2] gives $dX_t=(-7/2+3/2)X_tdt+\sqrt3X_t\,dW_t=-2X_tdt+\sqrt3X_t\,dW_t$ and $X_0=1$. The coefficients are globally Lipschitz, so [F1] identifies this with the unique strong solution. For $t>0$, completing the square in the $N(0,t)$ density gives $\mathbb E e^{uW_t}=e^{u^2t/2}$; at $t=0$ both sides are $1$. Hence $\mathbb E|X_t|^2=e^{-7t}\mathbb E e^{2\sqrt3W_t}=e^{-7t}e^{6t}=e^{-t}$.

Let $Y_n$ be explicit Euler with $h=1/2$. Since $b(x)=-2x$ and $\sigma(x)=\sqrt3x$, [F4] gives $Y_{n+1}=\sqrt3Y_n\Delta W_n$. Conditional on $\mathcal F_{t_n}$, independence and variance $h$ imply $\mathbb E(|Y_{n+1}|^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}) =3h|Y_n|^2=\tfrac32|Y_n|^2.$ Without the noise term, the deterministic multiplier is $1-2h=0$, so the factor greater than one here is caused by the stochastic increment.

For drift-implicit Euler, the resolvent equation is $Y_{n+1}+2hY_{n+1}=Y_n+\sqrt3Y_n\Delta W_n$. At $h=1/2$ this gives $Y_{n+1}=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt3\Delta W_n)Y_n$. Hence $\mathbb E(|Y_{n+1}|^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}) =\tfrac14(1+3h)|Y_n|^2=\tfrac58|Y_n|^2.$ The factor is strictly below one, so iteration gives $\mathbb E|Y_n|^2\le(5/8)^n|Y_0|^2$. The implicit resolvent exists because $x\mapsto x+2hx$ is bijective. AC is exactly [A1].
